reference.source: Mulliken and Young's Vascular Anomalies: Hemangiomas and Malformations
clinicalPearls: Rare disorder characterised by multifocal venous malformations of the skin and gastrointestinal tract.
Cutaneous lesions are soft, compressible, blue-black rubbery nodules that refill after compression and are often present from infancy.
Gastrointestinal venous malformations cause chronic occult bleeding with iron-deficiency anaemia and can bleed acutely anywhere from mouth to anus.
Usually sporadic and associated with somatic (rarely germline) TEK (TIE2) mutations.
The small bowel is frequently involved, making capsule endoscopy and deep enteroscopy valuable.
Lesions may also involve the liver, spleen, central nervous system and other organs.
Sirolimus (mTOR inhibitor) can reduce lesion size, bleeding and transfusion requirements.
Management is multidisciplinary, with endoscopic and surgical treatment targeting dominant bleeding lesions.
reference.pathophysiology: Blue rubber bleb naevus syndrome is a venous malformation disorder in which multiple thin-walled, dysplastic venous channels develop in the skin, gastrointestinal tract and viscera. Most cases are sporadic and driven by somatic activating mutations in the endothelial receptor TIE2 (TEK), which promote PI3K/AKT signalling and abnormal venous channel formation. The gastrointestinal lesions bleed readily because of their thin walls and mucosal location, producing chronic blood loss and iron-deficiency anaemia. The condition is distinguished from hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia and from isolated venous malformations by its characteristic multifocal cutaneous and gut distribution.
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and iron studies showing iron-deficiency anaemia
Video capsule endoscopy and device-assisted enteroscopy for the small bowel
MRI to map visceral and soft-tissue lesions
redFlags: Acute gastrointestinal haemorrhage with haemodynamic instability
Intussusception or volvulus arising from bowel lesions
Central nervous system lesions with neurological symptoms
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy is usually normal with appropriate management, but chronic gastrointestinal bleeding causes significant morbidity and transfusion dependence. Sirolimus has substantially improved control of bleeding in many patients.
pitfalls: Overlooking the gut as the source of unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia in a patient with blue skin nodules.
Attempting to resect every gastrointestinal lesion rather than targeting dominant bleeders.
Missing small-bowel lesions with standard endoscopy alone.
Confusing the condition with hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia.
references: Case series and reviews of blue rubber bleb naevus syndrome
